habitat: Singly or in pairs in any woodland and mixed bushveld. By day it perches close to a trunk, depresses its feathers, raises its ear tufts and half-closes its eyes.
summary: A common resident. The only very small owl with ear tufts. The plumage resembles tree bark. The grey morph is commoner than the brown morph, and both are mottled grey-brown with flecks of white and black. The call is a soft prrrrp at about ten-second intervals. The Kemp name Scops Owl and the code RB were left unchanged.

head.pattern: Small ear tufts. The grey morph is commoner than the brown morph. The plumage resembles tree bark, mottled grey-brown with flecks of white and black.

upperparts.pattern: Mottled grey-brown, like tree bark, with flecks of white and black.

viewNotes.note: Small ear tufts and bark-like mottling. It may half-close its eyes.
Mottled grey-brown with flecks of white and black. It can look long and thin.
The underside in flight is not described.

calls.description: A soft 'prrrrp', mostly at night and sometimes by day, repeated at about ten-second intervals. The grade A call is from Kruger. The filename is XC361285-African Scops-Owl (Otus senegalensis).mp3.

research.note: Newman calls it a common resident, and Avibase does not mark it rare, so all twelve months are listed. Grey-brown is not stored as one colour, and the grey and brown morphs are not given separate colour tokens. The grade A call is from Kruger. The Kemp name Scops Owl and the code RB were left unchanged.

population.notes: Kemp et al. 2001 order-of-magnitude threshold 2^14=16384 mature individuals (resident breeder); paper interval half–double → 8192–32768.
